questions.enonce_markdown:
Why did the League of Nations fail to maintain World Peace in the 1930s? What were the aims of the UNO that replaced the League in 1945? In what ways is the UN different from the defunct League of Nations?

(7/7/6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The League of Nations was created in 1920 to keep peace and organise collective security. It failed to prevent the aggression of the 1930s and was replaced in 1945 by the United Nations Organisation (UNO). The answer has three parts.

**(a) Why the League failed in the 1930s [7 marks].**
1. *Absence of major powers.* The United States never joined, because the Senate refused to ratify the Versailles Treaty; Germany was admitted in 1926 and left in 1933; Japan and Italy left in the 1930s; the USSR joined only in 1934 and was expelled in 1939.
2. *No army.* The League depended on its members to supply troops for enforcement, and they did not.
3. *Weak sanctions.* Economic sanctions were hard to apply when powers kept trading, and they were not applied firmly. During the Abyssinian crisis oil was not included in the sanctions and the Suez Canal stayed open to Italy.
4. *The unanimity rule.* Decisions in the Council and the Assembly needed agreement, which made quick action impossible.
5. *Self-interest of Britain and France.* They were weakened after the war, were concerned with their own interests and their empires, and preferred appeasement to a confrontation with the dictators.
6. *The Great Depression.* Economic crisis made countries turn to national self-interest and encouraged extremist and aggressive governments.
7. *The failures:* Manchuria (1931, Japan invaded; the Lytton Report condemned it; Japan simply left the League in 1933); Abyssinia (1935-1936, Italy invaded; the Hoare-Laval plan was a betrayal); the Disarmament Conference (1932-1934) failed; Hitler's breaches of the Treaty of Versailles (the Rhineland, 1936) went unpunished.

**(b) Aims of the United Nations [7 marks].** The UN Charter was signed at San Francisco in June 1945, and the UN began on 24 October 1945. Its aims are:
1. To maintain international peace and security and take effective measures against threats and acts of aggression.
2. To develop friendly relations among nations, based on equal rights and the self-determination of peoples.
3. To achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems.
4. To promote and respect human rights and fundamental freedoms for all, without distinction of race, sex, language or religion.
5. To serve as a centre for harmonising the actions of nations in pursuit of these common ends.
6. To help the progress of dependent peoples toward self-government through the Trusteeship system.
7. To work for disarmament, the peaceful settlement of disputes and the respect for international law.

**(c) How the UN differs from the League [6 marks].**
1. *Membership.* The UN includes nearly every state in the world, including the USA, the USSR (Russia), China, Britain and France, whereas the League lacked several great powers.
2. *Powers to use force.* The UN Security Council can order sanctions and military action and can send peacekeeping forces (Chapter VII of the Charter), while the League had no armed force of its own.
3. *Voting.* The League's decisions needed unanimity; in the UN the General Assembly votes by a majority and the Security Council by majority with the five permanent members (USA, USSR, UK, France, China) holding a veto.
4. *Specialised agencies.* The UN has many agencies (WHO, FAO, UNESCO, UNICEF, ILO and others), and a Secretary-General with a stronger role.
5. *Trusteeship.* The Trusteeship Council replaced the League mandate system, with wider aims of independence and with UN supervision.
6. *Organisation and base.* The UN has its headquarters in New York (the League in Geneva), a stronger International Court of Justice and a better financial basis.

**Conclusion.** The League failed because it lacked powers, members and the will of the great powers; the UN was built to avoid these errors, though the veto and the Cold War have limited it.
